Session 21 · Final DevOps Project

StockWise

An inventory app, taken from a laptop to a monitored Kubernetes cluster

Shubham Shah · Roll No. 10316

Slide 1 notes: Hi, I’m Shubham. This is StockWise, my final DevOps project. It’s a working inventory app, and around it I built the full toolchain from the course: tests, Docker, a CI/CD pipeline with security gates, Kubernetes with Helm, monitoring, GitOps and Terraform.

The application

A store’s stock, at a glance

Staff add products, track stock as goods arrive and ship, and see at a glance what needs reordering.

FastAPI · React · PostgreSQL

7 product endpoints + health

16 tests · 98% coverage

Slide 2 notes: The app is deliberately realistic: it has search and filters, stock adjustment that can’t go below zero, and a stats endpoint. The layout also works on phones. Tests run against SQLite so they never touch the real database.

Architecture

From a git push to a running cluster

The pipeline builds and checks every change. Argo CD then deploys whatever version Git says, and Prometheus watches it run.

Slide 3 notes: Walk the diagram left to right: developer, GitHub, the pipeline stages, the registry, Argo CD, then the cluster. Point out that the pipeline writes the new image version into Git, and Argo CD picks it up from there. Terraform on the right provisions the AWS cluster.

Slide 5 notes: Read the pills left to right. Tests and the security checks run first in parallel. The images are built once and scanned with Trivy. DevSecOps

Five checks, and any one can stop a release

SAST · Bandit and CodeQL read our code

SCA · pip-audit and npm audit check libraries

Secrets · Gitleaks scans every file

Images · Trivy blocks HIGH and CRITICAL

Gate · nothing is pushed unless all pass

Caught by Trivy

42 → 0

HIGH vulnerabilities in the frontend image. They came from old Alpine packages in the nginx base image, such as OpenSSL (CVE-2026-14456), not from my code. Patching the base image cleared all 42.

Slide 6 notes: The first Trivy scan failed the gate with 42 HIGH findings. The example to explain is CVE-2026-14456, a denial of service flaw in OpenSSL 3.5.6 inside the base image. The fix was apk upgrade in the Dockerfile, and the rescan was clean. The backend image was clean from the start.

Kubernetes and Helm

One Helm chart deploys the whole app

Backend · 2 to 5 pods

Frontend · 2 pods

PostgreSQL · 1Gi volume

Ingress · / and /api routes

Probes, Secret, migration Job

Slide 7 notes: Everything is in one chart: Deployments for backend and frontend, a StatefulSet for PostgreSQL with its own volume, ClusterIP Services, an Ingress, a ConfigMap, a Secret with a random password, an autoscaler, and a Job that runs the database migration once per release. Readiness checks the database, so a broken version never receives traffic.

Autoscaling under load

2 → 5 pods

During a load test, backend CPU reached 298% of its target. The autoscaler added pods up to the maximum of 5, then removed them once traffic stopped.

Slide 8 notes: The autoscaler compares CPU use with each pod’s CPU request of 100m. The load test sent parallel requests through the Ingress. You can see the rescale events in the screenshot. Scale-down happens automatically a few minutes after the load stops.

Monitoring

Prometheus scrapes every pod, Grafana shows it

Prometheus finds all 5 backend pods through a ServiceMonitor.

A 12-panel Grafana dashboard covers traffic, errors, latency, CPU, memory and replicas.

Slide 9 notes: The backend exposes /metrics. kube-prometheus-stack runs Prometheus, Grafana and Alertmanager in the cluster. Four alert rules watch for the backend being down, a high error rate, high latency and restarting pods.

GitOps

Git decides what runs in the cluster

git push

CI tests and scans

CI commits new tag

Argo CD syncs

New pods roll out

Self-heal

A manual change in the cluster is undone automatically.

Prune

Anything deleted from Git is deleted from the cluster.

Rollback

Reverting the tag commit redeploys the previous version.

Slide 10 notes: After a green pipeline, a bot commit writes the new image tag into the Helm values file. Argo CD notices the commit and syncs. Nobody runs helm upgrade by hand, and the Git history shows exactly which version is live.

Infrastructure as Code

Terraform describes the AWS cluster

VPC · 10.30.0.0/16 across 2 zones

Subnets · 2 public and 2 private

NAT gateway · outbound for private nodes

EKS · Kubernetes 1.34 cluster

Node group · 2 to 4 t3.medium

Workflow

terraform init
terraform fmt
terraform validate
terraform plan
terraform apply
terraform destroy

No credentials in the code. State and terraform.tfvars stay out of Git.

Slide 11 notes: Terraform uses the official VPC and EKS community modules. Worker nodes sit in private subnets and reach the internet through one NAT gateway, which keeps cost down. EKS and NAT bill by the hour, so destroy right after testing.

Troubleshooting challenge

Four failures, introduced on purpose and fixed

IncidentSymptomRoot causeFix
Bad image tagImagePullBackOffTag v9.9.9 never existedhelm rollback
Selector typoAPI returns HTTP 503Service matched no podsFix the selector
Wrong DB passwordPod Running, 0/1 ReadyPostgreSQL rejects the loginRestore the Secret
Too much memoryPod stuck Pending64Gi asked, node has 8Gihelm rollback

In every case the old pods kept serving traffic, because a new pod gets traffic only once it is Ready.

Slide 12 notes: Each incident followed the same steps: kubectl get pods, kubectl describe for the events, kubectl logs for the app’s own error, then the fix and a check. The wrong password case is the best one to show: the logs say password authentication failed, and the readiness probe kept the broken pod out of the Service.

Lessons learned

What building this taught me

Readiness protects users

Broken versions never got traffic.

Scanners find real issues

The 42 findings came from a base image.

Build once, ship that

The scanned image is the deployed one.

One owner for migrations

A Job runs Alembic once per release.

Git is the record

Deploys and rollbacks are commits.

Destroy what you create

Cloud resources bill by the hour.
